lines.text: A land of fire on the shores of the Caspian, of poets, oil barons and a long struggle over Karabakh. This is the story of Azerbaijan.
It starts with the Caspian Sea, a salty remnant of an ancient ocean, millions of years old, with oil and gas beneath its shores.
In the twelfth century, in the city of Ganja, the poet Nizami wrote Layla and Majnun, a love story still read across the Muslim world.
After Russia took the north, oil wells spread around Baku. By 1900 they gave half the world's oil, and the city boomed.
As the Russian Empire collapsed, a new Azerbaijan stepped onto the map in 1918.
Its Democratic Republic was the first republic of the Muslim world, until the Red Army took Baku two years later.
Heydar Aliyev was born. He would lead Soviet Azerbaijan, then rule the independent country, and found a ruling family.
His son Ilham was born in 1961, and would succeed him as president.
Two years later, Garry Kasparov was born in Baku. He would become world chess champion for fifteen years.
South of Baku, Gobustan became a protected reserve for its rock carvings of people, animals and boats, made over thousands of years.
In 1988 fighting broke out with Armenia over Nagorno-Karabakh, and grew into a war that Azerbaijan lost.
In January 1990, Soviet troops stormed Baku and killed scores of people. Within two years, Azerbaijan was independent.
Oil money flowed again when a new pipeline began carrying Caspian oil through Georgia and Turkey to the Mediterranean.
In Baku, three skyscrapers shaped like flames rose over the bay, a symbol of the land of fire.
In 2020, in a six-week war, Azerbaijan took back much of Karabakh.
And in September 2023 a final offensive took the rest, and nearly all of Karabakh's Armenians fled.
From Nizami's verses to the Flame Towers, Azerbaijan's story still burns bright by the Caspian.
